title: Before Adam — Node Learning Library
description: Contextual educational explanations, examples, units, experiments and caveats for the node inspector.

mass.title: Stellar mass
mass.meaning: The total amount of matter in a star. Mass sets the strength of gravity and strongly affects the star’s internal pressure, fusion rate and lifetime.

examples.name: Proxima Centauri
examples.explanation: Small red dwarf; burns hydrogen very slowly.

examples.name: Sirius A
examples.explanation: Hotter and more luminous than the Sun.

examples.name: Betelgeuse
examples.explanation: A red supergiant whose radius is hundreds of times the Sun’s.

mass.experiment: Try 0.5, 1 and 2 M☉. Compare gravity and fusion, then adjust other parameters to recover stability.
mass.modelLimitations: Mass is not the same as physical size. Betelgeuse is enormously wide but not hundreds of times the Sun’s mass.

radius.title: Stellar radius
radius.meaning: Distance from the centre of a star to its visible surface. Radius influences surface gravity and internal compression.

examples.name: Betelgeuse
examples.explanation: Its extended atmosphere makes its measured radius uncertain.

radius.experiment: Double radius while keeping mass fixed. Surface gravity falls to one quarter.
radius.modelLimitations: A star can expand enormously as it evolves without gaining a comparable amount of mass.

hydrogen.title: Hydrogen fraction
hydrogen.meaning: The fraction of stellar mass made of hydrogen, the main fuel for fusion in ordinary main-sequence stars.
hydrogen.unit: Mass fraction from 0 to 1; 0.70 means 70% hydrogen by mass.

examples.name: Hydrogen-depleted core
examples.explanation: Fusion converts hydrogen to helium in the core.

hydrogen.experiment: Compare 0.70 with 0.50 and inspect fusion output.
hydrogen.modelLimitations: The hydrogen fraction at a star’s surface need not equal the fraction in its core.

coreMK.title: Core temperature
coreMK.meaning: Temperature near a star’s centre, where nuclear fusion occurs.

examples.name: More massive main-sequence stars
examples.explanation: Hotter cores generally support faster fusion.

coreMK.experiment: Try 14, 15.7 and 18 MK and compare fusion output.
coreMK.modelLimitations: The model’s temperature-to-the-fourth-power fusion scaling is an approximation, not a universal law.

luminosity.title: Stellar luminosity
luminosity.meaning: The total power a star radiates. This differs from its apparent brightness, which depends on distance.

examples.name: Proxima Centauri
examples.explanation: Much less luminous than the Sun.

examples.name: Betelgeuse
examples.value: tens of thousands to over 100,000 L☉

luminosity.experiment: Increase luminosity without increasing fusion; inspect the thermal residual.
luminosity.modelLimitations: Luminosity is not the same as apparent brightness or surface temperature.

gravity.title: Surface gravity
gravity.meaning: The gravitational acceleration at the surface of a star, proportional to mass divided by radius squared.
gravity.experiment: Compare M = 1, R = 1 with M = 1, R = 2.
gravity.modelLimitations: The formula assumes a spherical star and uses the surface radius.

pressure.title: Gravitational compression
pressure.meaning: A simplified estimate of inward compression caused by gravity. In this classroom model it scales as M²/R⁴.
pressure.unit: Relative pressure, normalised to the Sun.

examples.name: Same mass, twice the radius
examples.explanation: Much weaker compression in this approximation.

pressure.experiment: Increase radius and compare compression with outward core pressure.
pressure.modelLimitations: Real stars have pressure gradients; this is not a detailed stellar structure model.

core.title: Core gas pressure
core.meaning: The outward pressure of hot gas, opposing the star’s gravitational compression.
core.unit: Relative pressure, normalised to the Sun.

examples.name: Solar reference
examples.explanation: The model’s benchmark for pressure balance.

core.experiment: Increase core temperature at fixed mass and radius.
core.modelLimitations: Real stars require an equation of state and a radial pressure profile.

fusion.title: Nuclear fusion
fusion.meaning: Fusion combines light atomic nuclei into heavier nuclei and releases energy that powers stars.

examples.name: Massive stars
examples.explanation: Often consume fuel much more rapidly.

fusion.experiment: Raise core temperature by 10% and observe the model’s response.
fusion.modelLimitations: This simplified scaling is not a complete nuclear reaction network.

hydro.title: Hydrostatic balance
hydro.meaning: A stable star needs outward pressure to balance the inward pull of gravity. This node measures their mismatch.

examples.name: Residual near zero
examples.explanation: The model’s inward and outward pressures agree.

hydro.experiment: Alter mass, then tune core temperature to reduce the mismatch.
hydro.modelLimitations: A small residual alone does not prove that a real star is stable.

thermal.title: Thermal balance
thermal.meaning: Over long periods, fusion power must broadly balance the energy the star radiates away.
thermal.experiment: Raise luminosity while keeping fusion unchanged.
thermal.modelLimitations: Real stars can temporarily store or release internal energy.

stable.title: Stellar stability
stable.meaning: Combines the hydrostatic and thermal residuals to assess whether the simplified star remains near equilibrium.

examples.name: Solar-like configuration
examples.explanation: A reference configuration that can satisfy the model.

stable.experiment: Find several different configurations with low residuals.
stable.modelLimitations: There is no unique best star; these are simplified classroom checks.

out.title: Stable star result
out.meaning: The output node displays the result of the connected star calculations. It does not calculate physics by itself.

examples.name: Complete and balanced graph
examples.explanation: All required equations and checks are connected and consistent.

out.experiment: Disconnect a wire, then reconnect it and observe the diagnostic.
out.modelLimitations: A displayed number alone does not establish physical validity.

temp.title: Water temperature
temp.meaning: Temperature of water or the surrounding environment; determines whether liquid water can persist.

examples.name: Earth average surface
examples.explanation: A broad global average, with wide regional variation.

temp.modelLimitations: The phase model is simplified; salinity and pressure affect freezing and boiling.

distance.title: Orbital distance
distance.meaning: The separation between a planet and its star. Received energy decreases with distance squared.

examples.name: Mars
examples.explanation: Receives less sunlight per square metre than Earth.

distance.experiment: Double the orbital distance; compare stellar flux and orbital speed.
distance.modelLimitations: Actual orbits are elliptical, so distance changes over time.

star.title: Star mass in an orbit
star.meaning: Mass of the central star whose gravity holds planets in orbit.
star.experiment: Increase central star mass while keeping orbital radius fixed.
star.modelLimitations: Circular orbital speed is a simplified two-body approximation.

capacity.title: Carrying capacity
capacity.meaning: The largest population that an environment can support under assumed resources and conditions.

examples.name: Small habitat
examples.explanation: Illustrative model setting, not a measured ecosystem.

examples.name: Larger habitat
examples.explanation: More resources may support more individuals.

capacity.modelLimitations: Real carrying capacity changes with food, climate, disease and competition.

rate.title: Population growth rate
rate.meaning: How rapidly a population increases in the logistic model before resource limits slow its growth.

examples.name: Higher rate
examples.explanation: Faster growth, potentially more unstable in discrete simulations.

rate.modelLimitations: This simple model ignores age structure, migration and ecological interactions.

phase.title: Water phase model
phase.meaning: Estimates whether water is solid, liquid or gas from temperature and pressure.

examples.name: Ice
examples.explanation: Typically solid at normal atmospheric pressure.

phase.experiment: Change temperature across freezing and boiling thresholds.
phase.modelLimitations: A full phase diagram is more complex.

orbit.title: Circular orbital speed
orbit.meaning: The speed required for a circular orbit around a central star at a chosen radius.

examples.name: Earth
examples.explanation: Mean orbital speed around the Sun.

orbit.experiment: Increase distance and observe orbital speed fall.
orbit.modelLimitations: Real orbital velocities vary along elliptical orbits.

flux.title: Stellar flux
flux.meaning: The amount of stellar power reaching each square metre at the planet’s orbit.

examples.name: Earth
examples.explanation: Solar irradiance near the top of Earth’s atmosphere.

flux.experiment: Double distance and see flux fall to one quarter.
flux.modelLimitations: Atmospheric absorption and reflectivity determine how much energy warms the surface.

population.title: Logistic population model
population.meaning: A simple model in which population growth slows as it approaches carrying capacity.
population.experiment: Increase growth rate and test for overshoot.
population.modelLimitations: Real populations can fluctuate or collapse; this is a simplified model.

frequency.title: Light frequency
frequency.meaning: How many wave oscillations occur each second. Frequency equals the speed of light divided by wavelength.
frequency.experiment: Change wavelength and observe frequency change inversely.
frequency.modelLimitations: The model assumes propagation in vacuum.

wavelength.title: Light wavelength
wavelength.meaning: Distance between successive peaks of a light wave; linked to colour for visible light.
wavelength.modelLimitations: Human colour perception depends on more than wavelength alone.

atmospheric-pressure.title: Atmospheric pressure
atmospheric-pressure.meaning: The force per unit area exerted by air. Pressure affects water’s boiling point and the ability of liquid water to persist.
atmospheric-pressure.experiment: Compare 1 atm with 0.02 atm at the same temperature.
atmospheric-pressure.modelLimitations: Pressure varies with altitude, weather and atmospheric composition.

planet-mass.title: Planetary mass
planet-mass.meaning: The total amount of matter in a planet. Together with radius it determines surface gravity.
planet-mass.experiment: Change mass from 1 to 2 M⊕ while holding radius fixed.
planet-mass.modelLimitations: Mass alone does not determine gravity without radius.

planet-radius.title: Planetary radius
planet-radius.meaning: Distance from a planet’s centre to its surface. Surface gravity decreases with radius squared at fixed mass.
planet-radius.experiment: Double radius while holding mass fixed.
planet-radius.modelLimitations: Planets with different densities have different mass–radius relationships.

add.title: Addition
add.experiment: Connect valid inputs and compare the result.
add.modelLimitations: This is a general mathematical operation; validity depends on its context.

multiply.title: Multiplication
multiply.meaning: Multiplies two quantities and combines their units.
multiply.experiment: Connect valid inputs and compare the result.
multiply.modelLimitations: This is a general mathematical operation; validity depends on its context.

divide.title: Division
divide.meaning: Divides one quantity by another; the divisor must not be zero.
divide.experiment: Connect valid inputs and compare the result.
divide.modelLimitations: This is a general mathematical operation; validity depends on its context.

sqrt.title: Square root
sqrt.meaning: Calculates the non-negative square root of an input.
sqrt.experiment: Connect valid inputs and compare the result.
sqrt.modelLimitations: This is a general mathematical operation; validity depends on its context.

expression.meaning: Evaluates the mathematical expression supplied by the player.
expression.experiment: Connect valid inputs and compare the result.
expression.modelLimitations: This is a general mathematical operation; validity depends on its context.

group.meaning: Groups calculations into a reusable subgraph.
group.experiment: Connect valid inputs and compare the result.
group.modelLimitations: This is a general mathematical operation; validity depends on its context.

display.title: Output display
display.meaning: Shows the value produced by the connected graph.
display.experiment: Connect valid inputs and compare the result.
display.modelLimitations: This is a general mathematical operation; validity depends on its context.
